summary: A proposal for a reconnection protocol, so one or both ends of a connection can move to another host. It gives examples such as TIP users using an executive program on a bigger host, presents a mechanism, sketches how it fits Host-Host or Telnet, and suggests where it belongs.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to carry on a phone call even if one person switches to a different phone partway through.

questions: moving a network connection to another host
subtitle: Moving a connection from one host to another without losing the session

tldr.problem: In some situations, users and programs need to move from one host to another without losing the connection or their session state.
tldr.mechanism: A reconnection mechanism using four commands (RRQ, ROK, RNO, RDO) allows one host to ask another to redirect a connection to a new destination. The protocol includes rules for handling simultaneous reconnection requests from both sides.
tldr.outcome: Programs can move between hosts transparently to users, enabling scenarios like executive programs handing off to other hosts, distributed simulations that reconfigure, and network authentication services.

today: This RFC proposes a protocol for transparent connection migration decades before it became common in modern systems. While not widely adopted in the early internet, the concept influenced later work on session mobility and mobile IP.

sections.title: When Reconnection Is Useful
sections.content: The RFC presents three examples where the ability to move a connection between hosts is valuable. First, a TIP user accessing an executive program on a larger host could be handed off to another host to do work, then passed back to the executive. Second, a centralized authentication service could validate a user's credentials and then pass the connection to their requested host. Third, distributed simulations like air traffic control systems can reconfigure by having program parts move from one computer to another while their connections follow.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you want to move to a different computer in the middle of what you are doing, like getting help at a central desk and then moving to your actual work computer.

sections.title: The Reconnection Mechanism
sections.content:
The mechanism uses four commands: RRQ (Reconnect Request), ROK (Reconnect OK), RNO (Reconnect No), and RDO (Reconnect Do). To move a connection, Host1 sends RRQ to Host2, Host2 responds with ROK, Host1 sends RDO with the destination host and port, and then Host2 breaks the old connection and initiates a new one to the destination. Host1 must arrange in advance for the destination host's cooperation by doing the same exchange with it.

Either party can refuse reconnection by responding with RNO. Once ROK is received by the requesting host, no more messages will arrive from the other side, ensuring no data is lost in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: The first host asks the second, the second agrees, then the first tells the second where to connect instead, and the second connects to the new place.

sections.title: Handling Simultaneous Requests
sections.content: If both hosts initiate reconnection to each other at the same time, a race condition occurs. The protocol resolves this by having both hosts use a comparison rule: each host computes a 40-bit number by concatenating a 32-bit socket number with an 8-bit site address. The host with the larger number gets to proceed first, while the other treats the incoming RRQ as either acceptance (ROK) or refusal (RNO) depending on the comparison result. This ensures a deterministic ordering and prevents deadlock.
sections.plainLanguage: If both computers try to move at the same time, they compare numbers to decide who goes first.

sections.title: Integration with Existing Protocols
sections.content: The reconnection mechanism can be added to the Host-Host protocol or to TELNET protocol. When added to Host-Host, the four commands are formatted with socket numbers. The RDO command for a send connection should not be sent until there are no messages in transit, and RDO is interpreted as implying a close (CLS) command.
sections.plainLanguage: The reconnection commands can fit into the existing network protocols that computers use to talk to each other.
